newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary central bank head sees interest rate fall.
newsitem.headline: Hungary central bank head sees interest rate fall.

text.p: Hungary's move to cut the monthly rate of the forint's devaluation will give a new impetus to the decline in interest rates, National Bank of Hungary (NBH) president Gyorgy Suranyi said on Monday.
The government decided on Sunday to reduce the monthly crawling peg devaluation rate to 1.1 percent from the current 1.2 percent, effective on April 1.
Suranyi told Hungarian Radio the beneficial impacts of the cut on interest rates are larger than the negative impact on the trade balance.

"When the inflation rate approaches the annual rate of devaluation and we do not slow the pace of devaluation, the negative impact that interest rates cannot drop further exceeds the favourable impact on exports and imports," he said.
Year-on-year inflation is running at 18.9 percent. Suranyi said last month that the year-on year consumer price index was likely to go down to some 17 percent by December 1997.
Hungary reduced inflation to an average 23.6 percent in 1996 from 28.2 percent in 1995, while government paper yields dropped almost 10 percent from above 30 percent.
The decline of interest rates slowed down since the end of January. Suranyi told the radio that a further drop in interest rates would not threaten savings.
He said current savings for one year offered a real yield of at least three to four percent.
"The yield on one-year government securities is still over 20 percent, while it is completely sure that one year from now (year-on-year) inflation will not be higher than some 16 percent."
The Hungarian government also decided on Sunday that Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy and Suranyi should work out a programme by the end of next month for reducing inflation.
Hungary has been urged by the International Monetary Fund to intensify its anti-inflationary efforts.
